pr_title: drivers: i2c: esp32: set timeout to allow clock stretching
pr_body:
The ESP32 series MCUs allow to set a timeout which triggers an error if the SCL line is unchanged for the specified amount of time.

By default, the ESP-IDF HAL sets the timeout to an arbitrary value of 10 times the bus cycle.

This is not sufficient for chips like the TI bq76952, which pulls the SCL line low (clock stretching) for several 100 µs.

The timeout should also not be dependent on the chosen bitrate, as it is defined by the time a chip needs for internal calculation before it can provide requested data or continue communication.

This commit adds a property to devicetree to allow configuration of the scl timeout. This value is set via direct register access, as the ESP-IDF HAL does not provide access to the enable bit and does not give any information about the maximum size of the timeout (defined in I2C clock cycles in the register).

Fixes #51351

## Remarks / Questions

1. As mentioned in the comment, the `I2C_TIME_OUT_EN` did not work as expected for the ESP32-C3. Maybe someone from Espressif can double-check internally if clearing this bit should disable the timeout. The communication only worked with the value set to `0x1F`. The documentation is not very detailed, so maybe my understanding is wrong.
2. The timeout value for ESP32-C3 is only 5 bits wide, which means that the maximum number of clock cycles can be `0x1F = 31`. With an I2C peripheral clock speed of 40 MHz, that would result in a maximum timeout of less than 1 µs, if my calculation is correct. However, in reality it does not time out for >200 µs (see logic analyzer screenshots in the issue). And if the maximum timeout was actually 1µs it would probably not be able to communicate with the bq76952 at all. What did I understand wrong? Or does using the maximum value actually completely disable the timeout feature?

issue_context.title: I2C: ESP32 driver does not support longer clock stretching
issue_context.body:
**Describe the bug**

I'm trying to make the ESP32-C3 talk to a TI bq76952 battery management IC (full hardware design [here](https://github.com/LibreSolar/bms-c1)). Exactly the same firmware works fine with an STM32G0B1. With the ESP32-C3 almost all I2C communication attempts fail.

Below an example of a failed I2C transaction to read the device ID:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/17674105/196286207-fa99db50-5f93-4142-a918-02dd703cd213.png)

The same command looks like this with the STM32.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/17674105/196286259-cdf61c91-3d13-4920-ae9b-91d367c1b3ef.png)

It can be observed that in both cases, the SCL is held low by the bq76952 towards the end (most probably because the device is busy with internal calculations). However, for the ESP32-C3 we suddenly see an 0xFF on the bus, which was not requested and does not belong there, whereas in case of the STM32 the communication continues after the clock stretching has finished.

**To Reproduce**

Custom board with ESP32-C3 and bq76952 is required, it will be difficult to reproduce with standard boards.

**Expected behavior**

The I2C communication handles clock stretching properly.

**Impact**

Communication with that chip does not work.

**Environment (please complete the following information):**

 - Commit SHA: f37ebf48ece1892771719321fca95156fd2e50c6
comments: I found a hacky solution to increase the timeout and fix the issue. Will come up with a PR in the next days.
@laurenmurphyx64 why do you think this is an enhancement? With the driver as it is now it is not possible to talk to the chip via I2C at all, so that's clearly a bug in my opinion.

@martinjaeger If I remember correctly, during the bug triage meeting this week folks were of the opinion that the expected behavior described in the bug was optional / not supported by Zephyr. It's possible we went too fast categorizing this one, though. @stephanosio Thoughts?

Yes, we don't have an API to configure the clock stretching / I2C timing behavior. But drivers should set values which are not configurable to conservative default values in such cases. Also configuration options can be added via devicetree without having a dedicated API (which I have done in the related PR).

review_comments: I will review this, but, have you checked `i2c_hal_set_tout()` function? It sets the i2C timeout and might be used in here instead. Not sure if this is only for slave operation though.

Yes, I did, but it does not allow to completely disable the timeout function using the `I2C_TIME_OUT_EN` bit mentioned in the reference manual. My initial goal was to use that bit to disable it by default. Unfortunately, this did not have any effect during my tests.

Also the HAL function does not perform any checks whether the value is too large or not. And it expects the value in number of clocks format instead of milliseconds or another time unit. So I decided to access the registers directly, as we need to get the maximum size of the value from the reg define and the clock frequency by other means anyways.

Did you want to limit the maximum timeout here? Doesn't seem bound anywhere other than by the shift. If timeout_cycles is large and a shift left is done the timeout could unexpectedly be quite low no?

It's already bound by the `MIN(a, b)` above, which limits the value to the maximum amount of bits allowed for that section of the register. Also the `I2C_TIME_OUT_REG_S` is actually 0 for all current ESP32 chips, but wanted to keep it generic.
